slides.title: Scramble and unscramble
slides.text: Encryption scrambles a message with a key, and decryption unscrambles it with the same key. A shift cipher moves every letter along by the key.
steps: D to G, O to R, G to J
slides.alt: The wheel at work: letters are shifting along the alphabet by the key, turning plain words into code.

focus.cue: Delivered: a scrambled word, read and sent
Shift 3: the key that scrambled it

slides.title: Trying every key
slides.text: A shift cipher has only 25 possible keys, so trying them all is quick. That is brute force, and it only works because the key space is tiny.
slides.alt: A later cipher level: with so few keys, trying every one is a real way in — for a shift cipher.

focus.cue: An unknown shift: turn one step at a time
Only 25 shifts exist: trying them all is quick

slides.title: Hiding is not scrambling
slides.text: Steganography hides a message, for example inside a picture, but anyone who finds it can read it. Encryption scrambles it, so finding it is not enough without the key.
slides.alt: Another cipher level on the wheel: scrambling with a key, which is stronger than merely hiding a message.

focus.cue: A key card swaps every letter for a partner
The secret message only the card can read

slides.title: End to end, with limits
slides.text: With end-to-end encryption, only the sender and receiver can read a message. Even the service carrying it cannot. It still cannot protect someone who is tricked into handing over the plain words.
slides.alt: The two-key lockbox card: anyone can click it shut, but only the owner holds the key that opens it.

focus.cue: The two-key lockbox: only the owner holds the opening key
Easy to crack, or hard to crack: sort the four ways

slides.title: The Magpie scrambles too
slides.text: The Magpie has started scrambling its own notes with a little wheel. It wishes it had not taught you how wheels work, because now you can spot its tricks.
slides.alt: Crack it by counting: a scrambled message, the Caesar wheel, and a button that counts how often letters appear.

focus.cue: A long scramble, and the reading it makes so far
Count the letters: the commonest letter is usually E

slides.title: Your mission
slides.text: Open Packet Post at Secret Messages and finish 4 levels. Use the wheel to unscramble each message, and think about how many keys a trickster would have to try.
slides.alt: Secret Messages in Pro: the cipher wheel waits with a scrambled message only the key can open.
